name: foma
why: A finite-state compiler and toolkit for building morphological transducers, a rare look at how computational linguistics encodes language as automata.

brief.what_it_is: foma is a finite-state compiler and C library for building finite-state transducers, the automata used in computational morphology. The README itself is very short and only says "Finite-state transducer technology." The rest of this description comes from the brew formula and scout notes, not the README. The README says the demo page lets you test foma regular expressions in a browser, so regular expressions appear to be the input language. The brew package installs three executables: foma, flookup, and cgflookup. The README does not describe what they do.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no stated motivation or problem framing beyond the one-line description. The scout notes frame it as a way to see how computational linguistics encodes language as automata.

commands_seen.context: Configure the build, as written in the README's compilation steps. This is the README's wording as given; cmake normally takes a source directory rather than a file path.

brief.install_notes: The README's native build requires the GNU readline library. The steps are: install readline, cd into foma, run cmake CMakeLists.txt, run make, and optionally run make install. The WebAssembly build does not need readline or zlib. It needs the Emscripten SDK installed and activated, followed by emcmake cmake and emmake make. Then serve the directory locally and open demo.html in a browser. No accounts are mentioned.
brief.standout: The WebAssembly build comes with an in-browser demo page for testing regular expressions, which is an unusual touch for a tool of this kind. The project is also a C library, so it can be embedded in other programs.
brief.status: Unknown. The GitHub mirror shows 313 commits, 136 stars, and 97 forks. The wiki page is described as "Automatically exported from code.google.com/p/foma," which suggests the code moved from Google Code. I could not find a release date or last-commit date in the pages I fetched.
brief.caveats: The README is very thin. It does not explain the language, the regular expression syntax, or what the three executables do. The native build needs GNU readline, and the README says nothing about Windows. The README's cmake invocation looks unusual and may not work as written. The wiki URL returned the repository page, not wiki content, so the docs I could reach were limited. The demo page only runs locally after the WebAssembly build.
quotes: The demo page allows you to test Foma regular expressions directly in your browser.
The `readline` and `zlib` dependencies are not needed for the wasm build.

judge.reason: Foma opens a distinctive door into computational morphology, compiling language rules into finite-state transducers rather than merely offering another developer utility.

entry.title: foma
entry.tldr: A finite-state compiler for building transducers, the machines computational linguists use to turn words into their parts and back again.
entry.deeper_look:
foma compiles regular expressions into finite-state transducers, which are automata that read one string and write another. In computational morphology, that lets a single machine map a surface word like "running" to an analysis, and run the same machine in reverse to generate words. The README is one line: "Finite-state transducer technology." Everything below that line comes from the package listing and the scout's notes.

The Homebrew package installs three executables: `foma`, `flookup`, and `cgflookup`. The README does not say what they do. Going by the names, `foma` is the interactive compiler and the other two look up words in compiled machines, but that is inference, not documentation. The project is also a C library, so the same machinery can be embedded in other programs.

The idea underneath is that a lot of language structure, such as inflection, stems, and sound changes, can be written as regular expressions and compiled into automata. It is a different way to think about language than parsing or statistical models, and it is a door into a long tradition of rule-based linguistics tooling. The repository says its wiki was exported from code.google.com/p/foma, so the project is old enough to have started on Google Code.

entry.whats_unique: It is a working finite-state toolkit that is also an embeddable C library. It can be built to WebAssembly, with a demo page for testing regular expressions in a browser.
entry.caveats: The README is very thin and does not explain the regular expression syntax or what the three executables do, and the wiki was not reachable from the brief, so expect to find documentation elsewhere.
